about: The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed: the confession of Nicaea (325) as reworked and much enlarged in the form received under the name of the Council of Constantinople (381) — a form that also drops clauses Nicaea had (the anathemas, “of the substance of the Father”). The Latin Mass text is a third form again: it keeps “Deum de Deo”, which the conciliar Greek does not have, and confesses the Spirit's procession “from the Father and the Son” (Filióque) — a Western addition, not in the Greek of the council. It entered the Roman Mass late: Berno of Reichenau reports that Rome began to sing it in 1014, when Benedict VIII conceded it at the request of Emperor Henry II — the usual account, though an earlier witness heard it at Rome around 800.

s01.narrative: At the middle of the altar the priest intones the profession of faith; the Credo is said on Sundays and greater feasts and usually omitted on weekdays. At the word “Deum” the priest bows his head to the cross, likewise at “Iesum Christum” and “simul adorátur”, and at the end, at “Et vitam ventúri sǽculi”, he signs himself with the cross.

s02.translation: I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.

s03.translation: And in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God.

s04.translation: And born of the Father before all ages.

s05.translation: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.

s06.translation: Begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father: through whom all things were made.

s07.translation: Who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven.

s08.narrative: The rubric calls for a genuflection here: the priest kneels from “Et incarnátus est” until “Et homo factus est” — honoring the moment the Incarnation is confessed; the faithful genuflect with him.

s09.translation: And was incarnate by the Holy Spirit, of the Virgin Mary: and was made man.

s10.translation: Crucified also for us: under Pontius Pilate he suffered and was buried.

s11.translation: And rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures.

s12.translation: And ascended into heaven: he sits at the right hand of the Father.

s13.translation: And he will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead: and of his kingdom there will be no end.

s14.translation: And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life: who proceeds from the Father and the Son.

s15.translation: Who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified: who spoke through the Prophets.

s16.translation: And in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.

s17.translation: I confess one baptism for the remission of sins.

s18.translation: And I await the resurrection of the dead.

s19.translation: And the life of the world to come. Amen.

w001.function: “Crédere in” with the accusative — “to believe *into* someone”, to entrust oneself — is biblical and Church syntax; classical Latin said “crédere” with the dative: to give credence.

w027.function: The participle agrees with “Fílium” (w021) — the chain of accusative appositions about the Son runs through several verses.

w042.function: The accusative appositions continue; set against “factum” (w044) it carries the heart of the Nicene confession: begotten, not made.

w045.function: It takes the dative “Patri” (w046): consubstantial with whom — with the Father.

w050.function: With “sunt” (w051) it forms the perfect passive: facta sunt — “were made”.

w060.function: The form looks the same in the present and the perfect; here it narrates the accomplished descent — “came down”.

w064.function: With “est” (w065) it forms the perfect: incarnátus est — “was made flesh”; Latin builds such tenses from a participle and the verb “to be”.

w074.function: Again a participle with “est” (w075): factus est — “was made”; the predicate is the nominative “homo” (w073).

w076.function: Three participles — crucified, “passus” (w083), “sepúltus” (w085) — are carried by one shared “est” (w086) at the end of the sentence.

w083.function: Participle of a deponent verb — passive form, active meaning: the one who suffered.

w090.function: The form “tértia” (w089) is feminine — “dies” is feminine here; the ablative answers: when?

w094.function: Like “descéndit” (w060): a form shared by present and perfect, here perfect — “ascended”.

w103.function: The future participle with “est” (w104): ventúrus est — “is to come, will come”; Latin's way of stating what is appointed.

w107.function: An infinitive of purpose after “ventúrus est”: he will come — to do what? — to judge. Classical prose would say “ad iudicandum”; the infinitive here is a Grecism, ordinary in biblical Latin.

w111.function: A possessive genitive with “regni” (w112); masculine, for the antecedent is Christ, not the kingdom — the form itself does not show the gender.

w122.function: A present participle serving as a title: literally “the one giving life”.

w126.function: The “-que” leaning on the word — an enclitic, not an ending — means “and”: ex Patre Filióque — “from the Father and the Son”.

w138.function: A deponent participle with “est” (w139): locútus est — “spoke”; passive form, active meaning.

w161.function: The future participle in the genitive, agreeing with “sǽculi” (w162): literally “of the age that is to come”.
